e.etymology: Has more than one source. Sanskrit Reva is an old name of the sacred Narmada river. In early 1900s America it was probably a form of Reba or Riva, pet forms of Rebecca.

assoc.t: Reva, the Third Sister in Star Wars: Obi-Wan Kenobi

e.etymology: An American coinage, apparently a blend of names such as Kevin and Trevor. It peaked in the early 1990s with R&B singer Tevin Campbell.
In the US mostly a spelling of Amy, from Old French Amee, 'beloved'. Ami is also a Japanese girls' name written with various characters, and a Hebrew boys' name meaning 'my people'.

assoc.t: ami, the French word for friend

e.etymology: The English word, from sun plus shine. As a given name it dates mostly from the 1970s, when word and nature names came into fashion.

assoc.t: You Are My Sunshine, the well-known lullaby song
sunshine, a term of endearment, sometimes sarcastic
the Sunshine State, Florida's nickname
Little Miss Sunshine, 2006 comedy film

e.note: Also an everyday pet name and a sarcastic form of address, as in 'listen, sunshine'.

e.etymology: A modern American respelling of Aleah or Aliyah with the -eigh of Leigh. Those names go back to Arabic Aliya, 'high, exalted', and overlap with Hebrew aliyah, 'ascent'.
From the English occupational surname for a collier, a maker or seller of charcoal and later a coal miner, from Middle English col, 'coal'.

assoc.t: Collier County, Florida, home of Naples
Collier's, the former American weekly magazine
collier, the word for a coal miner or a coal ship

e.etymology: A spelling of Zane, an American surname of uncertain origin that Western novelist Zane Grey made familiar as a first name. It also overlaps with Arabic Zain, 'beauty, grace'.

assoc.t: sounds like Zayn, the former One Direction singer

e.etymology: A modern respelling, most often of Aliza, a Hebrew name meaning 'joyful'. Some parents use it as a variant of Alyssa or Eliza.
A modern American spelling of the word name Navy, as in navy blue, with the -ie ending of Sadie and Millie.

assoc.t: sounds like navy, the sea force and the dark blue color

e.etymology: A compressed spelling of Kalani, from Hawaiian ka lani, 'the heavens' or 'the sky', a word also used of high chiefs.
e.note: Can be misread as KLAN-ee, since the spelling begins with Klan.

e.etymology: From French deja, 'already', known in English from the phrase deja vu. It caught on as an American girls' name in the 1990s.

assoc.t: deja vu, the feeling of having lived a moment before

e.etymology: A blend of Rose, from Latin rosa, and Anna, from the Hebrew for 'grace', in use in English since the 1700s. Toto's 1982 hit Rosanna lifted it in the US.

assoc.t: Rosanna, Toto's 1982 hit song

e.meaning: high, ascended (as a form of Eli)
e.etymology: Either a spelling of Eli, Hebrew for 'high' or 'ascended', or the surname taken from the English cathedral city of Ely, whose Old English name is of uncertain origin.

assoc.t: Ely, cathedral city in eastern England
Ely, Minnesota, gateway town to the Boundary Waters

e.etymology: From Greek amarysso, 'to sparkle'. Amaryllis is a shepherdess in the pastoral poems of Theocritus and Virgil, and the showy winter-blooming flower was named after her.

assoc.t: amaryllis, the red holiday flowering bulb

e.etymology: A modern American name of unclear origin, close in sound to Amani and Imani.
A modern respelling of Raya using Rae. Raya has several sources, among them Hebrew raya, 'friend', and a Slavic pet form of Raisa. Disney's 2021 film Raya and the Last Dragon raised its profile.

assoc.t: Raya, heroine of Disney's Raya and the Last Dragon

e.etymology: A spelling of Haisley, a recent American name that follows the sound of Paisley and Hadley. Haisley also exists as a rare surname.

e.meaning: from Our Lady of Lourdes, a title of the Virgin Mary
e.etymology: From Lourdes, the town in the French Pyrenees where Bernadette Soubirous reported visions of the Virgin Mary in 1858. Spanish speakers took Maria de Lourdes, then Lourdes alone, as a given name.
namesakes: Lourdes Leon (model and musician, daughter of Madonna)

assoc.t: Lourdes, the Catholic pilgrimage site in France

e.etymology: From alpha, the first letter of the Greek alphabet, used in English for a first child or a beginning. In West Africa, Alpha (or Alfa) is also a title for a Muslim scholar that became a common boys' name.

assoc.t: alpha, the first letter of the Greek alphabet
alpha, as in alpha male: the dominant one in a group
Generation Alpha, children born since the early 2010s

e.note: Reads first as the word: the Greek letter, alpha male, Gen Alpha.

e.etymology: The Russian and Romanian form of Andrew, from Greek Andreas, built on aner, 'man'. Saint Andrew the apostle carried the name across the Christian world.
A German short form of Nikolaus, from Greek Nikolaos: nike, 'victory', plus laos, 'people'. It is the same name as the Claus in Santa Claus.
namesakes: Klaus Mikaelson (vampire in The Vampire Diaries and The Originals)
Klaus Baudelaire (A Series of Unfortunate Events)

assoc.t: Santa Claus, whose Claus is the same name
Klaus, 2019 Netflix animated Christmas film
Klaus, the Original vampire of The Vampire Diaries

e.note: Close to the Claus of Santa Claus, so expect Santa jokes every December.

e.etymology: A recent American coinage: the -ayden sound of Jayden, Kayden and Zayden with a fashionable initial X.

assoc.t: Xaden Riorson, hero of the Fourth Wing novels

e.etymology: From Irish fiadh, the older spelling of fia, 'deer', from Old Irish fiad, 'wild, game'. A new given name in Ireland in the 2000s, it is now among the top girls' names there.
e.note: The Irish spelling trips up most Americans; it is said FEE-uh, with a silent dh.

e.etymology: A respelling of Jacqueline, the French feminine of Jacques, from Hebrew Yaakov (Jacob), who was born grasping his twin brother's heel. On its face it reads as Jack plus -lyn.
A modern spelling of Carly, a pet form of Carla and Caroline, feminine forms of Carl, from Germanic karl, 'free man'.
A respelling of Mia, which began as a Scandinavian and German pet form of Maria and also means 'mine' in Italian and Spanish. The -iyah ending follows Aaliyah.

e.meaning: hard stone used to strike fire
e.etymology: From the English word flint, Old English flint, the hard stone struck to make sparks. It is also a surname for someone who lived near a flint outcrop.
namesakes: Flint Lockwood (inventor hero of Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs)
Captain Flint (pirate of Treasure Island and Black Sails)

assoc.t: Flint, Michigan, the GM city known for its water crisis

e.note: Many Americans think first of Flint, Michigan, and the water crisis that began there in 2014.

e.etymology: From Persian zarin, 'golden', from zar, 'gold'. It is widely used across Central Asia, Russia and South Asia. Some hear in it tsarina, the title of a Russian empress.
A spelling of Jibril, the Arabic form of Gabriel, from Hebrew gever, 'strong man', and El, 'God'. In Islam, Jibril is the angel who brought the Quran to Muhammad.
A Hawaiian-style name ending in lani, 'heaven, sky', the element also found in Leilani and Kailani.
A modern American coinage in the style of Kyla and Nyla with an initial X. Some link it to Greek xylon, 'wood', the root of xylophone.
